nodes.name: Denis' reduction of PU learning to agnostic learning
nodes.statement: \citet{denis1990positive} introduced this model and showed that PU learning can be reduced to agnostic PAC learning, thereby establishing the classical VC-\mbox{dimension-based upper bound on its sample complexity.}
nodes.section: 1 Introduction
nodes.statement_short: PU learning reduces to agnostic PAC learning, giving the classical VC-dimension sample complexity bound.
conclusions: PU learning can be reduced to agnostic PAC learning
also_stated_at: \citet{denis1990positive} initiated the study from positive and unlabeled samples, showing that any class that is PAC-learnable is also PAC-learnable from positive and unlabeled samples (in the realizable setting). To show this, they reduced the (realizable) PAC-learnable from positive and unlabeled samples to learning in the CPCN model with noise bounded away from $\nfrac{1}{2}$.

nodes.name: PU learning model
nodes.statement:
In the PU learning model, one is given a concept class $\hypo{H}$ and access to two sample-streams:
\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=19pt,itemsep=0pt]
  \item[(a)] \textit{Unlabeled samples} drawn from a distribution $\customcal{D}^\star$ over the feature space, and 
  \item[(b)] \textit{Positive samples} drawn from a distribution $\customcal{P}^\star$, which corresponds to the conditional distribution of $\customcal{D}^\star$ restricted to the set ${H^\star} \coloneqq \{x : h^{\star}(x) = 1\}$ for some target concept $h^{\star} \in \hypo{H}$. 
\end{enumerate}  
That is, $\customcal{P}^\star$ is the truncation of $\customcal{D}^\star$ to the region where the label is positive.
nodes.section: 1.1 Learning with Positive and Imperfect Unlabeled Samples
nodes.statement_short: PU learning: unlabeled samples from D* and positive samples from D* truncated to the positive set H* of a target h*.

nodes.name: Generalized Smoothness
nodes.statement: There are known constants $\sigma \in (0,1]$ and $q\geq 1$, such that, for any measurable set $S$, $\customcal{D}^\star(S)\leq {(\nfrac{1}{\sigma})}\cdot \customcal{D}(S)^{\sfrac{1}{q}}$.
nodes.section: 1.1 Learning with Positive and Imperfect Unlabeled Samples
nodes.statement_short: D*(S) <= (1/sigma) D(S)^{1/q} for every measurable S.
nodes.label: asmp:smoothness

nodes.name: Non-Trivial Fraction of Positives
nodes.statement: For some known $\alpha>0$, $\Pr_{x\sim \customcal{D}^\star}\inparen{h^\star(x)=1}\geq \alpha$.
nodes.section: 1.1 Learning with Positive and Imperfect Unlabeled Samples
nodes.label: asmp:posFraction

nodes.name: Sample Complexity of PIU Learning
nodes.statement:
Suppose \cref{asmp:smoothness} holds. 
    Fix any $\varepsilon,\delta\in (0,\nfrac{1}{2})$.
    There is an algorithm that, given $\varepsilon,\delta$ and $n=\wt{O}\binparen{{{(\varepsilon \sigma)}}^{-2q}\cdot \inparen{\textrm{\rm VC}{}(\hypo{H})+\log{\nfrac{1}{\delta}}}}$ independent samples from $\customcal{P}^\star$ and $\customcal{D}$, outputs a hypothesis $\wh{h}$ such that, with probability $1-\delta$,
    \[ 
        \Pr_{\customcal{D}^\star}\binparen{\wh{h}(x)\neq h^\star(x)}\leq \varepsilon\,.
    \]
nodes.section: 1.2.1 Sample Efficient PIU Learning
nodes.statement_short: Under generalized smoothness, ~O((eps sigma)^{-2q}(VC(H)+log 1/delta)) samples suffice to PIU-learn to error eps.
assumptions: \cref{asmp:smoothness} holds
Fix any $\varepsilon,\delta\in (0,\nfrac{1}{2})$.
conclusions:
There is an algorithm that, given $\varepsilon,\delta$ and $n=\wt{O}\binparen{{{(\varepsilon \sigma)}}^{-2q}\cdot \inparen{\textrm{\rm VC}{}(\hypo{H})+\log{\nfrac{1}{\delta}}}}$ independent samples from $\customcal{P}^\star$ and $\customcal{D}$, outputs a hypothesis $\wh{h}$ such that, with probability $1-\delta$,
    \[ 
        \Pr_{\customcal{D}^\star}\binparen{\wh{h}(x)\neq h^\star(x)}\leq \varepsilon\,.
    \]
nodes.label: infthm:sampleComplexity

nodes.name: Computational Complexity of PIU Learning (informal)
nodes.statement:
Suppose \cref{asmp:smoothness,asmp:posFraction} hold. 
    Fix $\varepsilon,\delta\in (0,\nfrac{1}{2})$, and let $k$ be such that degree-$k$ polynomials $\zeta$-approximate $\hypo{H}$ in \mbox{$L_1$-norm} with respect to $\customcal{D}$ for $\zeta\leq \inparen{{\varepsilon\alpha}{\sigma}}^{\mathrm{poly}(q)}$.
    Then, there is an algorithm that, given $n=\mathrm{poly}(d^k,\nfrac{1}{\zeta},\log{\nfrac{1}{\delta}})$ independent samples from $\customcal{P}^\star$ and $\customcal{D}$, outputs a hypothesis $\wh{h}$ such such that, with probability $1-\delta$, 
    \[
        \Pr_{\customcal{D}^\star}\binparen{\wh{h}(x)\neq h^\star(x)}\leq \varepsilon\,.
    \]
    The algorithm runs in time $\mathrm{poly}(n)$.
nodes.section: 1.2.2 Computationally Efficient PIU Learning
nodes.statement_short: Informal: with smoothness and positive mass, L1 polynomial approximability w.r.t. D gives a poly(d^k,1/zeta) time PIU learner.
assumptions: \cref{asmp:smoothness,asmp:posFraction} hold

let $k$ be such that degree-$k$ polynomials $\zeta$-approximate $\hypo{H}$ in \mbox{$L_1$-norm} with respect to $\customcal{D}$ for $\zeta\leq \inparen{{\varepsilon\alpha}{\sigma}}^{\mathrm{poly}(q)}$
conclusions: The algorithm runs in time $\mathrm{poly}(n)$.
nodes.label: mainthm:algo

nodes.name: Natarajan's impossibility of proper learning from positive samples
nodes.statement: \citet{natarajan1987learning} characterized the classes that can be \textit{properly} PAC learned from only positive samples showing that even simple classes such as two-dimensional halfspaces are not properly learnable from positive samples alone.
nodes.section: 1.3.1 Learning with Smooth Positive Samples
conclusions: even simple classes such as two-dimensional halfspaces are not properly learnable from positive samples alone
also_stated_at: This intuition was formalized by \citet{natarajan1987learning}: Natarajan studied binary classification with \textit{only} positive samples (as our high-quality source provides) and showed that almost no hypothesis classes are learnable by any proper learner; indeed, even 2-dimensional halfspaces, cannot be learned from just positive examples.

nodes.name: Impossibility of Learning from Positive Samples
nodes.statement:
Let $\hypo{H}$ be any hypothesis class satisfying $\lim_{k\to\infty} \textrm{\rm VC}{}(\hypo{H}_{\cap k})=\infty$ where $\hypo{H}_{\cap k}$ is the hypothesis class formed by taking intersections of $k$ hypothesis from $\hypo{H}$, \textit{i.e.}{}, 
    $\hypo{H}_{\cap k}\coloneqq \inbrace{H_1\cap H_2\cap \dots\cap H_k\colon H_1,H_2,\dots,H_k\in \hypo{H}}.$
    
    For any (randomized) algorithm, there is an $h^\star\in \hypo{H}$ and distributions $\customcal{D},\customcal{D}^\star$ satisfying \cref{asmp:smoothness} and \cref{asmp:posFraction} with parameters $(\sigma,q,\alpha)=(\nfrac{1}{2},1,\nfrac{1}{2})$, such that given sample access to $\customcal{D}$ and $\customcal{P}^\star$ (the truncation of $\customcal{D}^\star$ to the set of positive samples), after any finite time, with probability $\nfrac{1}{2}$, 
    the algorithm outputs a hypothesis $\wh{h}$ such that, with probability $1-\delta$,
    \[ 
        \Pr_{\customcal{D}^\star}\binparen{\wh{h}(x)\neq h^\star(x)}\geq \Omega(1)\,.
    \]
nodes.section: 1.3.1 Learning with Smooth Positive Samples
nodes.statement_short: If VC of k-fold intersections of H is unbounded, no algorithm learns H from positive samples even with smoothness and positive mass 1/2.
assumptions: Let $\hypo{H}$ be any hypothesis class satisfying $\lim_{k\to\infty} \textrm{\rm VC}{}(\hypo{H}_{\cap k})=\infty$
conclusions: there is an $h^\star\in \hypo{H}$ and distributions $\customcal{D},\customcal{D}^\star$ satisfying \cref{asmp:smoothness} and \cref{asmp:posFraction} with parameters $(\sigma,q,\alpha)=(\nfrac{1}{2},1,\nfrac{1}{2})$
nodes.label: thm:impossibilityPositiveSamples

nodes.name: Proof of Informal Corollary 1.4
nodes.statement: An immediate corollary of \cref{thm:sampleComplexity} and \cref{infthm:main} is  an affirmative answer to this.
nodes.section: 1.3.1 Learning with Smooth Positive Samples
nodes.statement_short: Immediate from the sample-complexity and computational PIU results.

nodes.name: Learning from smooth positive samples (informal)
nodes.statement:
Consider a PAC learning instance with class $\hypo{H}$, feature distribution $\customcal{D}^\star$ that is $(\sigma,q)$-smooth (for $\sigma=\Omega(1)$; see \cref{asmp:smoothness}) with respect to a known reference $\customcal{D}$ that one can efficiently sample from, and target $h^\star\in \hypo{H}$.  
    \begin{itemize}
        \item[$\triangleright$] \textit{(Sample Complexity)} ~~
            $\wt{O}\sinparen{{\varepsilon^{-2q}}\cdot \inparen{\textrm{\rm VC}{}(\hypo{H}) + \log{\nfrac{1}{\delta}}}}$ independent positive samples are sufficient to $(\varepsilon,\delta)$-PAC learn $\hypo{H}$ with respect to $\customcal{D}^\star$.
        \item[$\triangleright$] \textit{(Computational Complexity)}~~
            Suppose $\customcal{D}^\star({H^\star})\geq \Omega(1)$.
            Let $k\geq 1$ be such that $\hypo{H}$ is $\varepsilon^{O(q)}$-approximable by degree-$k$ polynomials in the $L_1$-norm with respect to $\customcal{D}$.
            Then, $n=\mathrm{poly}(d^k,\nfrac{1}{\varepsilon},\log{\nfrac{1}{\delta}})$ positive samples and $\mathrm{poly}(n)$ time is sufficient to $(\varepsilon,\delta)$-PAC learn $\hypo{H}$ with respect to $\customcal{D}^\star$.
    \end{itemize}
nodes.section: 1.3.1 Learning with Smooth Positive Samples
nodes.statement_short: Positive samples alone suffice to PAC learn H when D* is smooth w.r.t. a known samplable reference D.
assumptions: feature distribution $\customcal{D}^\star$ that is $(\sigma,q)$-smooth (for $\sigma=\Omega(1)$; see \cref{asmp:smoothness}) with respect to a known reference $\customcal{D}$ that one can efficiently sample from
conclusions: $\wt{O}\sinparen{{\varepsilon^{-2q}}\cdot \inparen{\textrm{\rm VC}{}(\hypo{H}) + \log{\nfrac{1}{\delta}}}}$ independent positive samples are sufficient to $(\varepsilon,\delta)$-PAC learn $\hypo{H}$ with respect to $\customcal{D}^\star$.
nodes.label: infcor:smooth_classification

nodes.name: List Decoding PIU Model
nodes.statement:
Fix a distribution $\customcal{D}^\star$ over domain $\customcal{X}$ and numbers $\ell,q\geq 1$ and $\sigma\in (0,1]$.
    In the List Decoding model specified by parameters $(\customcal{D}^\star,\ell,\sigma,q)$, one is provided a list of $\ell$ distributions $\customcal{D}_1, \customcal{D}_2, \dots, \customcal{D}_\ell$ over $\customcal{X}$ such that for some \textit{unknown} index $1\leq i^\star\leq \ell$,
    $\customcal{D}_{i^\star}$ is $(\sigma,q)$-smooth with respect to $\customcal{D}_{i^\star}$ in the sense of \cref{asmp:smoothness}. 
    The distributions ${{\customcal{D}}}_j$ (for $j\neq i^\star$) can be arbitrary.
nodes.section: 1.3.2 Learning with Positive Samples and Lists of Unlabeled Samples
nodes.statement_short: A list of l distributions is given, one unknown member of which D* is smooth with respect to; others are arbitrary.
nodes.label: def:list

nodes.name: PIU learning in the List Decoding model (informal)
nodes.statement:
Consider a PAC learning instance with      
        class $\hypo{H}$,
        feature distribution $\customcal{D}^\star$, and 
        target $h^\star\in \hypo{H}$.  
    Consider the corresponding instance of the List Decoding PIU Model in \cref{def:list} with $\sigma=\Omega(1)$ and $\ell=O(1)$ and parameter $q\geq 1$.
    \begin{itemize}
        \item[$\triangleright$] \textit{(Sample Complexity)}~~ 
            $\wt{O}\inparen{\varepsilon^{-2q}\cdot \inparen{\textrm{\rm VC}{}(\hypo{H})+\log{\nfrac{1}{\delta}}}}$ independent positive samples are sufficient to $(\varepsilon,\delta)$-PAC learn $\hypo{H}$ with respect to $\customcal{D}^\star$.
        \item[$\triangleright$] \textit{(Computational Complexity)}~~
            Suppose $\customcal{D}^\star({H^\star})\geq \Omega(1)$.
            Let $k\geq 1$ be such that $\hypo{H}$ is $\zeta$-approximable by degree-$k$ polynomials in the $L_1$-norm with respect to $\customcal{D}_{i^\star}$ for $\zeta\leq \varepsilon^{\,O(q)}$.
            Then, $n=\mathrm{poly}(d^k,\nfrac{1}{\zeta},\log{\nfrac{1}{\delta}})$ positive samples and $\mathrm{poly}(n)$ time is sufficient to $(\varepsilon,\delta)$-PAC learn $\hypo{H}$ with respect to $\customcal{D}^\star$.
    \end{itemize}
nodes.section: 1.3.2 Learning with Positive Samples and Lists of Unlabeled Samples
nodes.statement_short: Informal: with a list of O(1) unlabeled distributions, sample and computational complexity match the PIU case.
assumptions: Consider the corresponding instance of the List Decoding PIU Model in \cref{def:list} with $\sigma=\Omega(1)$ and $\ell=O(1)$ and parameter $q\geq 1$.
conclusions: $\wt{O}\inparen{\varepsilon^{-2q}\cdot \inparen{\textrm{\rm VC}{}(\hypo{H})+\log{\nfrac{1}{\delta}}}}$ independent positive samples are sufficient to $(\varepsilon,\delta)$-PAC learn $\hypo{H}$ with respect to $\customcal{D}^\star$.
nodes.label: infthm:list

nodes.name: Obtaining a List of Distributions From Adversarially Corrupted Data
nodes.statement: In this remark, we show that if one is given adversarially corrupted unlabeled samples, then one can satisfy the guarantees of the above list-decoding model. Suppose that $\customcal{D}^\star$ is a Gaussian distribution $\customcal{N}(\mu^\star,\Sigma^\star)$. Consider a data source that is $(1-\gamma)$-corrupted for some $\gamma\in (0,1]$: with probability $\gamma$, the source outputs a sample from $\customcal{D}^\star$, and, otherwise with probability $1-\gamma$, it outputs an arbitrary sample that may depend on the past samples and the knowledge of the learning algorithm. In \cref{sec:advCorruption}, we show that one can efficiently convert an $(1-\gamma)$-corrupted source for any $\gamma>0$, into one satisfying the requirements of the List Decoding PIU Model with $\ell= \mathrm{poly}(\nfrac{1}{\gamma})$. Moreover, under mild assumptions, we also extend this to the case where $\customcal{D}^\star$ is an exponential family distribution.
nodes.section: 1.3.2 Learning with Positive Samples and Lists of Unlabeled Samples
nodes.statement_short: A (1-gamma)-corrupted Gaussian source can be converted to a List Decoding PIU instance with poly(1/gamma) distributions.
nodes.label: rem:list

nodes.name: Three-phase algorithm for truncated estimation with unknown survival set
nodes.statement:
The state-of-the-art algorithm for this problem \cite{lee2024unknown} works in three phases:
        \begin{enumerate}[itemsep=0pt]
            \item \textit{Phase 1:}~ First, it finds an unlabeled density $\customcal{D}$ close to $\customcal{D}^\star$ (in the sense of \cref{asmp:smoothness});
            \item \textit{Phase 2:}~ Then, it learns $S$ such that the symmetric difference $\customcal{D}^\star(S\triangle S^\star)\approx 0$; and 
            \item \textit{Phase 3:}~ Finally, it recovers $\theta^\star$ using  learned set $S$.
nodes.section: 1.3.3 Truncated Estimation with Unknown Survival Set
nodes.statement_short: Find a smooth unlabeled density, learn the survival set, then estimate theta* from the learned set.

nodes.name: Proof of Informal Corollary 1.7
nodes.statement: The bottleneck in their algorithm is Phase 2 which falls under the setting of \cref{infthm:main} and, substituting the algorithm in Phase 2 by the algorithm in \cref{infthm:main} gives us the following improvement upon \citet{lee2024unknown}'s result.
nodes.section: 1.3.3 Truncated Estimation with Unknown Survival Set
nodes.statement_short: Replace Phase 2 of Lee et al.'s algorithm by the efficient PIU learner.

nodes.name: Truncated Estimation with Unknown Survival Set (informal)
nodes.statement:
Let the family $\hypo{D}=\inbrace{\customcal{D}(\theta)\colon \theta}$ satisfy the assumptions of \cite{lee2024unknown} and let $\alpha=\Omega(1)$. 
            Fix any $\varepsilon, \delta \in (0, \nfrac{1}{2})$, and let $S^\star$ be $\mathrm{poly}(\varepsilon)$-approximable by degree-$k$ polynomials in $L_1$-norm with respect to $\hypo{D}$.
            There is an algorithm that given $n = \mathrm{poly}(d^k, \nfrac{1}{\varepsilon}, \log{\nfrac{1}{\delta}})$ independent samples from $\customcal{D}(\theta^\star)$ truncated to $S^\star$ 
            outputs parameter $\wh{\theta}$ such that with probability $1-\delta$, 
            \[ \tv{\customcal{D}(\wh{\theta})}{\customcal{D}(\theta^\star)} \leq \varepsilon\,.\]
            The algorithm runs in time $\mathrm{poly}(n)$.
nodes.section: 1.3.3 Truncated Estimation with Unknown Survival Set
nodes.statement_short: Informal: exponential-family parameters can be estimated in TV from samples truncated to an unknown L1-approximable set.
assumptions: Let the family $\hypo{D}=\inbrace{\customcal{D}(\theta)\colon \theta}$ satisfy the assumptions of \cite{lee2024unknown} and let $\alpha=\Omega(1)$.
let $S^\star$ be $\mathrm{poly}(\varepsilon)$-approximable by degree-$k$ polynomials in $L_1$-norm with respect to $\hypo{D}$
conclusions: The algorithm runs in time $\mathrm{poly}(n)$.
nodes.label: infcor:truncation

nodes.name: Detecting truncation
nodes.statement: In particular, to the problem of testing whether a given set of samples is i.i.d.{} from a distribution $\customcal{Q}$ or i.i.d.{} from the truncation $\customcal{Q}(S^\star)$ of $\customcal{Q}$ to some unknown set $S^\star$.
nodes.section: 1.3.4 Detecting Truncation
nodes.statement_short: Test whether samples are i.i.d. from Q or from Q truncated to an unknown set S*.

nodes.name: Conditions (C1)-(C3) of De et al. for detecting truncation
nodes.section: 1.3.4 Detecting Truncation
nodes.statement_short: Q hypercontractive, an i.i.d. product distribution, and with an exactly computable orthonormal polynomial basis.

nodes.name: Detecting Truncation (informal)
nodes.statement:
Consider the setting described above with $\beta=\Omega(1)$.
            Suppose one has an efficient sampling oracle for $\customcal{Q}$.
            Fix any $\delta\in (0,\nfrac{1}{2})$ and $k\geq 1$ such that $S^\star$ is $O(1)$-approximable by degree-$k$ polynomials in the $L_1$-norm with respect to $\customcal{Q}$.
            There is an algorithm that given $n=d^{k}\cdot \mathrm{polylog}({\nfrac{1}{\delta}})$ samples from $\customcal{Q}$ or $\customcal{Q}(S^\star)$, with probability $1-\delta$, correctly detects whether the samples were from $\customcal{Q}$ or $\customcal{Q}(S^\star)$ in $\mathrm{poly}(n)$ time.
            
            Moreover, the algorithm also works (with the same guarantees) with an \emph{approximate} sampling oracle--that outputs samples from a distribution $\customcal{R}$ such that $\customcal{Q}$ is $(\sigma,q)$-smooth (for $q=O(1)$ and $\sigma=\Omega(1)$; see \cref{asmp:smoothness}) with respect to $\customcal{R}$. 
            (In particular, it is sufficient to have $\chidiv{\customcal{R}}{\customcal{Q}}=O(1)$; \cref{lem:closenessFromChiSquare}.)
nodes.section: 1.3.4 Detecting Truncation
nodes.statement_short: Informal: truncation by an L1-approximable set is detectable with d^k polylog(1/delta) samples, even with approximate sampling.
assumptions: Suppose one has an efficient sampling oracle for $\customcal{Q}$.
conclusions: There is an algorithm that given $n=d^{k}\cdot \mathrm{polylog}({\nfrac{1}{\delta}})$ samples from $\customcal{Q}$ or $\customcal{Q}(S^\star)$, with probability $1-\delta$, correctly detects whether the samples were from $\customcal{Q}$ or $\customcal{Q}(S^\star)$ in $\mathrm{poly}(n)$ time.
nodes.label: infcor:detectingTruncation

nodes.name: Mixture distribution M of the PU-to-agnostic reduction
nodes.statement:
The resulting feature distribution is a mixture of the form (for some weight $\gamma\in (0,1)$):
            \[
                \customcal{M} = \gamma \customcal{P}^\star + (1-\gamma) \customcal{D}\,.
                \addtocounter{equation}{1}\tag{\theequation} \]
nodes.section: 1.4.1 Challenges in Using Existing Approaches for PIU Learning
nodes.statement_short: M = gamma P* + (1-gamma) D, obtained by labelling all unlabeled samples negative.

nodes.name: Two-sided strengthening of generalized smoothness
nodes.statement:
To illustrate additional challenges in obtaining computationally efficient algorithms, let's suppose that $\customcal{D}$ satisfies the following strengthening of \cref{asmp:smoothness}: for all measurable sets $S$,
            \[
                \customcal{D}^\star(S)
                    \leq O(\customcal{D}(S)^{1/q})
                \qquadtext{and}
                \customcal{D}^\star(S)
                    \geq \Omega(\customcal{D}(S)^{q})
                \,,
                \addtocounter{equation}{1}\tag{\theequation} \]
nodes.section: 1.4.1 Challenges in Using Existing Approaches for PIU Learning
nodes.statement_short: D*(S) <= O(D(S)^{1/q}) and D*(S) >= Omega(D(S)^q) for all measurable S.

nodes.name: Two-sided smoothness makes ERM succeed
nodes.statement: These requirements turn out to be sufficient to ensure that ${H^\star}$ is (close to) the optimal solution of the agnostic learning problem created above and, hence, to ensure that ERM learns ${H^\star}$.
nodes.section: 1.4.1 Challenges in Using Existing Approaches for PIU Learning
conclusions: ${H^\star}$ is (close to) the optimal solution of the agnostic learning problem created above

nodes.name: L_q approximation w.r.t. D transfers to L_1 approximation w.r.t. P*
nodes.statement:
Using this, one can show that if $p\colon\mathbb{R}^d\to \mathbb{R}$ $\varepsilon$-approximates a hypothesis $h$ with respect to $\customcal{D}$ in $L_q$-norm for the constant $q$ from \textup{\tagform@{\ref{eq:bounded_chisquare}}}, 
                then it is an $O(\varepsilon)$-approximating polynomial with respect to $\customcal{P}^\star$ in $L_1$-norm.

conclusions: it is an $O(\varepsilon)$-approximating polynomial with respect to $\customcal{P}^\star$ in $L_1$-norm

nodes.name: Uniform mixture of the list is smooth for D*
nodes.statement: This approach is promising since one can show that $(\customcal{D}^\star,\customcal{M})$ satisfies \cref{asmp:smoothness} with $\sigma'=\sigma \ell^{-1/q}$ and $q'=q$: indeed, for any measurable set $S$, we have $\customcal{M}(S)^{1/q}\geq \ell^{-1/q}\customcal{D}_{i^\star}(S)^{1/q}\geq \sigma\ell^{-1/q}\customcal{D}^\star(S)$, where the last inequality holds as $(\customcal{D}^\star,\customcal{D}_{i^\star}$) satisfies \cref{asmp:smoothness}.
nodes.section: 1.4.3 Learning in the List Decoding PIU Model
conclusions: $(\customcal{D}^\star,\customcal{M})$ satisfies \cref{asmp:smoothness} with $\sigma'=\sigma \ell^{-1/q}$ and $q'=q$

nodes.name: Polynomial-time PIU learning for halfspaces and intersections of halfspaces
nodes.statement:
Is there an algorithm that in the PIU learning model finds an $\wh{h}$ satisfying the guarantee of \cref{thm:main} in $\mathrm{poly}(\nfrac{d}{\varepsilon})$  time for the following concept classes $\hypo{H}$ and distributions $(\customcal{D}^\star,\customcal{D})$?
            \begin{itemize}[itemsep=0pt]
                \item[$\triangleright$] $\hypo{H}$ is the intersections of $O(1)$ halfspaces and $\sinparen{\customcal{D}^\star,\customcal{D}}$ are unknown Gaussian distributions; and 
                \item[$\triangleright$] $\hypo{H}$ is a single halfspace and $\sinparen{\customcal{D}^\star,\customcal{D}}$ are arbitrary distributions.
            \end{itemize}

nodes.name: Indicator notation
nodes.statement: Given a point $x\in \mathbb{R}^d$ and a set $S\subseteq\mathbb{R}^d$, we use $\mathds{1}_S(x)$ and $\mathds{1}\{x \in S\}$ to denote the indicator that $x\in S$.
nodes.section: 2 Preliminaries

nodes.name: L_p norm of a vector
nodes.statement: For a vector $z\in \mathbb{R}^d$ and $p\geq 1$, the $L_p$-norm of $z$ is $\relax{z}_p\coloneqq \inparen{\sum_i \abs{z_i}^p}^{\sfrac{1}{p}}$ and, taking limit $p\to\infty$ implies, $\relax{z}_\infty=\max_i \abs{z_i}$.
nodes.section: 2 Preliminaries

nodes.name: Mass of a set under a distribution
nodes.statement: Given a distribution $\customcal{D}$ over $\mathbb{R}^d$ and a measurable set $S\subseteq\mathbb{R}^d$, $\customcal{D}(S)$ denotes the mass of $S$ under $\customcal{D}$, \textit{i.e.}{}, $\Pr_{x\sim \customcal{D}}[x\in S]$.
nodes.section: 2 Preliminaries

nodes.name: Truncation of a distribution to a set
nodes.statement: We overload this notation at times in applications in truncated statistics (in \cref{sec:intro:application,sec:application:unknownTruncation,sec:application:detectingTruncation}) to also mean the truncation of a distribution $\customcal{D}$ to the measurable set $S$, \textit{i.e.}{}, if ${\rm d}\customcal{D}$ is the density of $\customcal{D}$, $\customcal{D}(S)$ is the conditional distribution $\propto \mathds{1}_S(x) \cdot {\rm d}\customcal{D}(x)$.
nodes.section: 2 Preliminaries
also_stated_at: The truncation of a distribution $\customcal{D}$ to a set $S$ is the conditional distribution of $\customcal{D}$, conditioned on the event that a point lies in $S$. When $\customcal{D}$ has a density, the truncated density is given by $\frac{1}{\customcal{D}(S)} \cdot \mathds{1}\inparen{x \in S} \cdot \customcal{D}(x)$

nodes.name: Hypotheses as functions and sets
nodes.statement: We use both Boolean functions (\textit{e.g.}{}, $h\colon \mathbb{R}^d \rightarrow \inbrace{0,1}$) and sets $(H \subseteq \mathbb{R}^d)$ to denote hypotheses, with the relation $H = \inbrace{x \in \mathbb{R}^d \colon h(x) = 1}$.
nodes.section: 2 Preliminaries

nodes.name: Polynomial Threshold Functions (PTF)
nodes.statement:
Given $k\geq 1$, let $\hypo{P}(k)$ be the collection of all polynomial threshold functions of degree-$k$.
        A polynomial threshold function (PTF) of degree $k$ is a function defined by a polynomial $p\colon \mathbb{R}^d \rightarrow \mathbb{R}$ of maximum degree $k$ and a threshold $t \in \mathbb{R}$ in the following sense:
        $H({p,t})\coloneqq \mathds{1}\sinbrace{p(x)\geq t}$.
nodes.section: 2 Preliminaries
differentia: defined by a polynomial $p\colon \mathbb{R}^d \rightarrow \mathbb{R}$ of maximum degree $k$ and a threshold $t \in \mathbb{R}$
nodes.label: def:ptfs:polynomials

nodes.name: Distribution of positive covariates P*
nodes.statement: We use $\customcal{P}^\star$ to denote the distribution of positive covariates or features, which satisfies $\operatorname{supp}(\customcal{P}^\star)={H^\star}$.
nodes.section: 2 Preliminaries
also_stated_at: $\customcal{P}^\star$ and $\customcal{D}^\star$ are related: $\customcal{P}^\star$ is the truncation of $\customcal{D}^\star$ to ${H^\star}$ -- the set of positive examples.

nodes.name: Feature distribution D*
nodes.statement: $\customcal{D}^\star$ denotes the distributions of all features (regardless of whether their label is positive or not).
nodes.section: 2 Preliminaries

nodes.name: Total variation distance
nodes.statement: The total variation distance between $\customcal{P}$ and $\customcal{Q}$ is $\tv{\customcal{P}}{\customcal{Q}}=\inparen{\nfrac{1}{2}}\int_{x}\abs{{\rm d} \customcal{P}(x)-{\rm d} \customcal{Q}(x)}{\rm d} x$.
nodes.section: 2 Preliminaries

nodes.name: Chi-square divergence
nodes.statement:
The $\chi^2$ divergence from $\customcal{P}$ to $\customcal{Q}$ is  $\chidiv{\customcal{P}}{\customcal{Q}}
        = \int \inparen{\nfrac{{\rm d}\customcal{P}}{{\rm d}\customcal{Q}}}^2 {\rm d} \customcal{Q} - 1$.
nodes.section: 2 Preliminaries
also_stated_at: The $\chi^2$-divergence of $\customcal{P}$ with respect to $\customcal{Q}$ is $\chidiv{\customcal{P}}{\customcal{Q}}=\int_x \inparen{\nfrac{{\rm d} \customcal{P}(x)}{{\rm d} \customcal{Q}(x)}}^2 {\rm d} \customcal{Q}(x) - 1$.

nodes.name: Renyi divergence
nodes.statement: Similarly, the Rényi divergence of order \(r \geq 1\) from \(\customcal{P}\) to \(\customcal{Q}\) is defined as $\renyi{r}{\customcal{P}}{\customcal{Q}} = \frac{1}{r - 1} \log \int (\sfrac{{\rm d} \customcal{P}}{{\rm d} \customcal{Q}})^r {\rm d} \customcal{Q}$.
nodes.section: 2 Preliminaries

nodes.name: Domain of features
nodes.statement: To begin with, we have a domain $\customcal{X}$ of covariates or features that is a subset of $\mathbb{R}^d$, either discrete or continuous, and a distribution $\customcal{D}^\star$ over the domain.
nodes.section: 3.1 Learning with Positive and Imperfect Unlabeled Samples

nodes.name: Realizable labels
nodes.statement: We are interested in binary classification and operate in the realizable setting, where for each feature $x$ there is a corresponding label $y(x)\in \ensuremath{\inbrace{0, 1}}$, that is realized by an unknown Boolean function $h^\star\colon \customcal{X}\to \ensuremath{\inbrace{0, 1}}$.
nodes.section: 3.1 Learning with Positive and Imperfect Unlabeled Samples

nodes.name: Hypothesis class
nodes.statement: $h^\star$ can be arbitrary and the only assumption we make is that there is a known hypothesis class $\hypo{H}$ (which is a collection of Boolean functions $h\colon \customcal{X}\to \ensuremath{\inbrace{0, 1}}$) that contains $h^\star$.
nodes.section: 3.1 Learning with Positive and Imperfect Unlabeled Samples

nodes.name: Support of Positive Examples H*
nodes.section: 3.1 Learning with Positive and Imperfect Unlabeled Samples
also_stated_at: Given a hypothesis class $\hypo{H}$ and a target function $h^\star$, we use ${H^\star}$ -- which is the set corresponding to $h^\star$ -- to denote the set of positive examples.

nodes.name: Extensions to More General Notions of Smoothness
nodes.statement:
The techniques we use to bound the sample complexity and computational complexity of PIU learning extend beyond \cref{asmp:smoothness}.
                They suffice for PIU learning under the following weakening of \cref{asmp:smoothness}:
                there is a known rate function $r\colon \mathbb{R}_{\geq 0}\to \mathbb{R}_{\geq 0}$ satisfying $\lim_{m\to 0^+} r(m)=0$ such that the pair of distributions $\inparen{\customcal{D}, \customcal{D}^\star}$ satisfy
                \[
                    \text{for any measurable set $S$}\,,\quad 
                    r(\customcal{D}^\star(S))\leq \customcal{D}(S)\,.
                    \addtocounter{equation}{1}\tag{\theequation} \]
                This captures \cref{asmp:smoothness} when $r(m)=(\sigma m)^{q}$.
                This additional generality also allows our framework to extend to settings where we can only ensure $\kl{\customcal{D}^\star}{\customcal{D}}=O(1)$ (see \cref{sec:klBoundsSatisfyGeneralSmoothness} for details).
                This is important as \cref{asmp:smoothness} does not hold in this setting for any finite $\sigma$ or $q$.
                Regarding results under \textup{\tagform@{\ref{eq:mostGeneral:smoothness}}}, using our techniques one can deduce that the sample complexity of the PIU learning is $O\binparen{\mathrm{poly}{(r(\varepsilon))}\cdot \inparen{\textrm{\rm VC}{}(\hypo{H})+\log{\nfrac{1}{\delta}}}}$ and the computational complexity is $\mathrm{poly}(d^k,\nfrac{1}{\zeta},\log{\nfrac{1}{\delta}})$ for $\zeta\leq r(\mathrm{poly}(\alpha,\varepsilon))$.
nodes.section: 3.1 Learning with Positive and Imperfect Unlabeled Samples
nodes.statement_short: Results extend to smoothness via any rate function r with r(D*(S)) <= D(S); this covers bounded KL divergence.
nodes.label: rem:generalSmoothness

nodes.name: PIU Learning
nodes.statement:
An instance of PIU Learning is specified by a hypothesis $h^\star\in \hypo{H}$, that induces a set of positive samples ${H^\star}$ (\cref{eq:setOfPositiveExamples}), a distribution $\customcal{D}^\star$ of features, and a (low-quality) distribution $\customcal{D}$ that is close to $\customcal{D}^\star$ as specified by \cref{asmp:smoothness}.
            One has access to two streams of samples:
            \begin{enumerate}
                \item \emph{(High-quality Stream)}\quad Samples $x_1,x_2,\dots \sim \customcal{P}^\star$ where $\customcal{P}^\star$ is the truncation of $\customcal{D}^\star$ to ${H^\star};$ and 
                \item \emph{(Low-quality Stream)}\quad Samples $x_1,x_2,\dots \sim \customcal{D}$. 
            \end{enumerate}
            The goal is to output a hypothesis $h\colon \customcal{X}\to \ensuremath{\inbrace{0, 1}}$ such that, with high probability, $h$ is close to $h^\star$ in the usual sense of PAC-learning: with probability $1-\delta$, $\Pr_{\customcal{D}^\star}\inparen{h^\star(x)\neq h(x)} \leq \varepsilon.$
nodes.section: 3.1 Learning with Positive and Imperfect Unlabeled Samples
nodes.statement_short: Learn h* to error eps under D* from positive samples (D* truncated to H*) and unlabeled samples from a smooth surrogate D.
nodes.label: prob:PUlearning

nodes.name: Polynomial Approximability
nodes.statement:
Fix a concept $h\colon \mathbb{R}^d \to \inbrace{0,1}$, distribution $\customcal{D}$ over $\mathbb{R}^d$, numbers $k,p\geq 1$, and constant $\varepsilon>0$.
                $h(\cdot)$ is said to be $\varepsilon$-approximable by degree-$k$ polynomials in $L_p$-norm with respect to $\customcal{D}$ if there exists a degree-$k$ polynomial $f\colon \mathbb{R}^d\to\mathbb{R}$ such that 
                \[
                    \inparen{\operatornamewithlimits{\mathbb{E}}_{x\sim \customcal{D}}{\abs{f(x)-h(x)}^p}}^{\sfrac{1}{p}} < \varepsilon\,.  
                \]
                (For sets, we simply replace $h(x)$ with the indicator of the set, \textit{i.e.}{}, $\mathds{1}_H(x)$.)
                Moreover, a hypothesis class $\hypo{H}$ is said to be $\varepsilon$-approximable by degree-$k$ polynomials in $L_p$-norm with respect to a family of distributions $\hypo{D}$ if, for each $h\in \hypo{H}$ and $\customcal{D}\in \hypo{D}$, $h$ is  $\varepsilon$-approximable by degree-$k$ polynomials in $L_p$-norm with respect to $\customcal{D}$.
nodes.section: 3.1 Learning with Positive and Imperfect Unlabeled Samples
nodes.statement_short: h is eps-approximable if some degree-k polynomial f has (E_D|f-h|^p)^{1/p} < eps; a class is if every member is.
nodes.label: def:poly_approx

nodes.name: L2-approximability implies L1-approximability
nodes.statement: It is worthwhile to note that if a hypothesis is approximable in $L_2$-norm, then it is also approximable in the $L_1$-norm because for any random variable $Z$, $\operatornamewithlimits{\mathbb{E}}[\abs{Z}]\leq \sqrt{\operatornamewithlimits{\mathbb{E}}[Z^2]}$.
nodes.section: 3.1 Learning with Positive and Imperfect Unlabeled Samples
assumptions: a hypothesis is approximable in $L_2$-norm
conclusions: it is also approximable in the $L_1$-norm

nodes.name: Robust Denis reduction of Lee, Mehrotra and Zampetakis
nodes.statement:
A recent work \cite{lee2024unknown} designed a robust version of \citet{denis1990positive}'s reduction from PU learning to agnostic learning that works when $\customcal{D}\neq \customcal{D}^\star$ but the pair $(\customcal{D},\customcal{D}^\star)$ satisfy \cref{asmp:smoothness} and an additional assumption (see \cref{asmp:densityLB}).
        This results in a sample complexity of {$O(\textrm{\rm VC}{}(\hypo{H})\cdot \varepsilon^{-2(1+q)})$}.
nodes.section: 3.2 Main Results for PIU Learning
assumptions: the pair $(\customcal{D},\customcal{D}^\star)$ satisfy \cref{asmp:smoothness} and an additional assumption (see \cref{asmp:densityLB})
conclusions: This results in a sample complexity of {$O(\textrm{\rm VC}{}(\hypo{H})\cdot \varepsilon^{-2(1+q)})$}.

nodes.name: Proper vs. Improper Learning
nodes.statement:
The learner in \cref{thm:sampleComplexity} is improper: it outputs a hypothesis that is an intersection of $(\nfrac{1}{\varepsilon})$-hypotheses in our original class. 
            This is necessary as simple examples show that proper PIU learning is impossible (\cref{rem:necessityOfImproper}).
nodes.section: 3.2 Main Results for PIU Learning

nodes.name: Computationally Efficient Algorithm for PIU Learning
nodes.statement:
Let \cref{asmp:smoothness,asmp:posFraction} hold.
            Fix any $\varepsilon,\delta\in (0,\nfrac{1}{2})$ and $k$ such that degree-$k$ polynomials $\zeta$-approximate $\hypo{H}$ with respect to $\customcal{D}$ in $L_1$-norm for $\zeta\leq O(\alpha^{8q})\cdot (\sigma\varepsilon\alpha)^{5q^2}$.
            Then, there is an algorithm (\cref{alg:main}) that, given 
                any $\varepsilon,\delta\in (0,1)$, 
                the constants $\sigma,q$ from \cref{asmp:smoothness},and 
                $n=\mathrm{poly}(d^k,\nfrac{1}{\zeta},\log{\nfrac{1}{\delta}})$ samples from each stream in PIU Learning model (\cref{prob:PUlearning}), 
            outputs a hypothesis ${h}\colon \customcal{X}\to\ensuremath{\inbrace{0, 1}}$ such that, with probability $1-\delta$, 
            \[
                \Pr_{\customcal{D}^\star}\inparen{{h}(x)\neq h^\star(x)}\leq \varepsilon\,.
            \]
            The algorithm runs in time $\mathrm{poly}(n)$.
nodes.section: 3.2 Main Results for PIU Learning
nodes.statement_short: With smoothness, positive mass alpha and zeta-L1-approximability w.r.t. D, a poly(d^k,1/zeta) time algorithm PIU-learns to error eps.
assumptions: Let \cref{asmp:smoothness,asmp:posFraction} hold.

Fix any $\varepsilon,\delta\in (0,\nfrac{1}{2})$ and $k$ such that degree-$k$ polynomials $\zeta$-approximate $\hypo{H}$ with respect to $\customcal{D}$ in $L_1$-norm for $\zeta\leq O(\alpha^{8q})\cdot (\sigma\varepsilon\alpha)^{5q^2}$.
conclusions: The algorithm runs in time $\mathrm{poly}(n)$.
nodes.label: thm:main

nodes.name: SQ Lower Bound
nodes.statement:
\citet{diakonikolas2024statistical} provide an SQ-lower bound for the -- seemingly -- unrelated task of Gaussian parameter estimation with samples truncated to an unknown set.
            However, if we can avoid the exponential dependence on $\nfrac{1}{\varepsilon}$ in \cref{thm:main} then, due to the recent results \cite{lee2024unknown}, we will also obtain a $\mathrm{poly}(\nfrac{d}{\varepsilon})$ time algorithm for the problem studied by \citet{diakonikolas2024statistical} thereby contradicting their lower bound.
            See \cref{sec:application:unknownTruncation} for further discussion of parameter estimation from truncated samples and how our results relate to it.
nodes.section: 3.2 Main Results for PIU Learning
nodes.statement_short: Avoiding the exponential 1/eps dependence would contradict the SQ lower bound of Diakonikolas et al. for truncated Gaussian estimation.
nodes.label: rem:SQlowerbound

nodes.name: Testing Approximability
nodes.statement:
\cref{thm:main} requires the hypothesis class $\hypo{H}$ to be approximable by polynomials with respect to $\customcal{D}$ in $L_1$-norm.
            Many guarantees on polynomial approximability are known with respect to specific distribution families such as Gaussians.
            One way to test this guarantee is to test whether the provided samples indeed come from a Gaussian distribution.
            However, most existing distributional testers have prohibitively large running time -- exponential in $d$ \cite{rubinfeld2023testing}.
            Instead, if $\hypo{H}$ satisfies a slightly stronger property that it has sandwiching polynomials with respect to the underlying distribution, then one can use Theorem 3.2 of \citet{gollakota2023momentMatching} that gives a tester that runs in $\mathrm{poly}(d^{k},\nfrac{1}{\varepsilon})$ time. 
            In particular, the tester comes with the following guarantees.
            \begin{enumerate}[itemsep=0pt]
                \item {(Completeness)}\quad It says \textsf{Yes} if samples are drawn from distribution $\customcal{D}$;
                \item {(Soundness)}\quad If this tester says \textsf{Yes} on samples $S$, then with high probability, $\varepsilon$-$L_1$-approximating polynomials exist with respect to the empirical distribution $\wh{\customcal{D}}$ over the samples $S$.\footnote{
                    To be precise, their result actually shows the existence of $L_1$-sandwiching polynomials, which is sufficient for us since $L_1$-sandwiching (whose definition is not relevant here) is a stronger requirement than $L_1$-approximation.
                }
            \end{enumerate}
            Now, we can run the algorithm in \cref{thm:main} with respect to the empirical distribution $\wh{\customcal{D}}$.
            To use \cref{thm:main}, we need to verify that $\customcal{D}^\star$ is smooth with respect to $\customcal{D}^\star$ in the sense of \cref{asmp:smoothness}.
            By standard VC theory for sufficiently large samples uniform convergence holds with respect to degree-$k$ polynomials, yielding the following additive-relaxation version of \cref{asmp:smoothness}:
            for any measurable set $T$, $\customcal{D}^\star(T)\leq (\nfrac{1}{\sigma}) \, \inparen{\smash{\wh{\customcal{D}}}(T)+\varepsilon}^{1/q}$.
            This weaker guarantee is sufficient to execute our proof as we only use assumption \cref{asmp:smoothness} \mbox{for sets $T$ whose mass is bounded away from $0$.}
nodes.section: 3.2 Main Results for PIU Learning
nodes.statement_short: Moment-matching testers for sandwiching polynomials can certify the L1-approximability needed by the main theorem.
nodes.label: rem:testing

nodes.name: Density Lower Bound
nodes.statement:
There are known constants $\sigma\in (0,1]$, such that, for any measurable set $S$, $\customcal{D}^\star(S)\geq 
                \sigma
                \cdot \customcal{D}(S).$
nodes.section: 3.2 Main Results for PIU Learning
nodes.label: asmp:densityLB

nodes.name: Density lower bound is much stronger than smoothness
nodes.statement:
While \cref{asmp:densityLB} is similar to \cref{asmp:smoothness}, it is substantially stronger: 
            \textit{e.g.}{}, when the (imperfect) unlabeled samples are gathered from an unreliable source, they are bound to contain some elements not in support of the true unlabeled distribution $\customcal{D}^\star$, and such elements are enough to violate \cref{asmp:densityLB}.
nodes.section: 3.2 Main Results for PIU Learning
nodes.label: rem:densityLB

nodes.name: Optimal Sample Complexity with Density Lower Bound
nodes.statement:
Suppose \cref{asmp:smoothness,asmp:densityLB} hold with $q=1$. 
            Fix any $\varepsilon,\delta\in (0,\nfrac{1}{2})$.
            There is an algorithm that, given $\varepsilon,\delta$ and $n=\wt{O}\binparen{\inparen{\nfrac{1}{\varepsilon\sigma}}^{-1}\cdot \inparen{\textrm{\rm VC}{}(\hypo{H})+\log{\nfrac{1}{\delta}}}}$ independent samples from $\customcal{P}^\star$ and $\customcal{D}$, outputs a hypothesis $\wh{h}$ such that, with probability $1-\delta$,
            \[ 
                \Pr_{\customcal{D}^\star}\binparen{\wh{h}(x)\neq h^\star(x)}\leq \varepsilon\,.
            \]
nodes.section: 3.2 Main Results for PIU Learning
nodes.statement_short: For q=1 with the density lower bound, ~O((VC(H)+log 1/delta)/(eps sigma)) samples suffice.
assumptions: \cref{asmp:smoothness,asmp:densityLB} hold with $q=1$
Fix any $\varepsilon,\delta\in (0,\nfrac{1}{2})$.
conclusions:
There is an algorithm that, given $\varepsilon,\delta$ and $n=\wt{O}\binparen{\inparen{\nfrac{1}{\varepsilon\sigma}}^{-1}\cdot \inparen{\textrm{\rm VC}{}(\hypo{H})+\log{\nfrac{1}{\delta}}}}$ independent samples from $\customcal{P}^\star$ and $\customcal{D}$, outputs a hypothesis $\wh{h}$ such that, with probability $1-\delta$,
            \[ 
                \Pr_{\customcal{D}^\star}\binparen{\wh{h}(x)\neq h^\star(x)}\leq \varepsilon\,.
            \]
nodes.label: thm:sampleComplexity:bothSided

nodes.name: Optimality of the q=1 sample complexity
nodes.statement: Note that this sample complexity is optimal for PIU learning (up to logarithmic factors), since it is optimal for realizable PAC learning which is an easier problem.
nodes.section: 3.2 Main Results for PIU Learning
conclusions: this sample complexity is optimal for PIU learning (up to logarithmic factors)

nodes.name: Pessimistic-ERM
nodes.section: 4 Proofs of Main Results for PIU Learning (thm:main,thm:sampleComplexity)
nodes.statement_short: Minimize the fraction of unlabeled samples in H over H in the class, subject to H containing a 1-rho fraction of positive samples.
also_stated_at:
This can be formalized as the following program: given sets $P$ and $U$ of positive and unlabeled samples and a tolerance $\rho\geq 0$ 
            \[
                \operatornamewithlimits{arg\,min}_{H\in \hypo{H}}~~ \frac{\abs{H\cap U}}{\abs{U}}
                \,,\quad\text{ such that}\,,\quad 
                \frac{\abs{H\cap P}}{\abs{P}} \geq 1-\rho
                \,.
                \tag{Pessimistic-ERM{}}
            \]

nodes.name: Second-Order Uniform Convergence
nodes.section: 4.1 Proof of 1.1 (Sample Efficient Algorithm)
nodes.statement_short: Empirical and true masses of F triangle F* agree up to sqrt(mass * s) + 4s, with s = (2 VC log(n+1) + log 4/delta)/n.
assumptions: Let $\hypo{F}$ be any concept class on $\mathbb{R}^d$ with finite VC-dimension, \textit{i.e.}{}, $\textrm{\rm VC}{(\hypo{F})}<\infty$, and let $\customcal{D}$ be any distribution over $\mathbb{R}^d$.
conclusions: with probability $1-\delta$, over the draw $X\sim \customcal{D}^n$, every $F\in \hypo{F}$,
nodes.label: thm:unifConvergence

nodes.name: Second-order uniform convergence: true mass bound
nodes.section: 4.1 Proof of 1.1 (Sample Efficient Algorithm)
nodes.label: eq:sampleComplexity:1

nodes.name: Second-order uniform convergence: empirical mass bound
nodes.section: 4.1 Proof of 1.1 (Sample Efficient Algorithm)
nodes.label: eq:sampleComplexity:2

nodes.name: Necessity of Improper Learners for PIU Learning
nodes.statement:
To illustrate that improper learners are necessary, consider the class of one-dimensional halfspaces (\textit{i.e.}{}, thresholds with a ``direction''). Define
        \[
        h_{\leq 1} = \{ x \in \mathbb{R} : x \leq 1 \} \qquadtext{and} h_{\geq -1} = \{ x \in \mathbb{R} : x \geq -1 \}\,.
        \]
        Let the two ``true" unlabeled distributions be 
        \[
            \customcal{D}^\star_1 = {\rm Unif}[-2,1] \qquadtext{and} \customcal{D}^\star_{-1} = {\rm Unif}[-1,2]\,.
        \]
        We now consider two PIU learning instances defined by (a): unlabeled distribution $\customcal{D}^\star_1$ with optimal hypothesis $h_{\leq 1}$ and (b): unlabeled distribution $\customcal{D}^\star_{-1}$ with optimal hypothesis $h_{\geq -1}$.
        Note that both instances yield the same positive sample distribution, $\customcal{P}^\star = {\rm Unif}[-1,1]$.
        Let the imperfect unlabeled distribution for both instances be $\customcal{D} = {\rm Unif}[-2,2]$; which satisfy \cref{asmp:smoothness} with parameters $(\sigma,q)=(\nfrac{3}{4},1)$ in both instances.
        Since any deterministic learner cannot distinguish between these two instances, if it is proper (\textit{i.e.}{}, its output is restricted to one-dimensional halfspaces), it must incur a constant error on at least one of the instances. The same holds with probability $\nfrac{1}{2}$ for randomized learners.

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 1.1
nodes.statement:
The algorithm is presented in \cref{alg:sampleComplexity}.
        It solves $T\coloneqq\nfrac{1}{\varepsilon}$ carefully selected instances of Pessimistic-ERM{} to obtain hypotheses $H_1,H_2,\dots,H_T$ and outputs $\bigcap_{i=1}^{T} H_i$.
        The instances of Pessimistic-ERM{} are constructed iteratively, where $i$-th problem removes all unlabeled samples not in $H_1 \cap H_2 \cap\dots \cap H_{i-1}.$
        \begin{algorithm}[htb!]
        \caption{\textsf{Iterative-Pessimistic-ERM{}} (from \cref{thm:sampleComplexity})}
        \begin{algorithmic}[1]
        \Procedure{\rm \textsf{Iterative-Pessimistic-ERM{}}}{$\varepsilon,\delta,\sigma,q,\hypo{H}$}
            \vspace{2mm}
            \State Set $n=\wt{O}\binparen{\inparen{\nfrac{1}{\varepsilon\sigma}}^{2q}\cdot \inparen{\textrm{\rm VC}{}(\hypo{H})+\log{\nfrac{1}{\delta}}}}$
            \State Obtain $n$ positive samples $P$ and $n$ (imperfect) unlabeled samples $U$
            \vspace{2mm}
            \State Set $T=\nfrac{1}{\varepsilon}$
            \vspace{2mm}
            \For{$1\leq i\leq T$}
                \State Define the survival set $S_i=H_1\cap H_2\cap\dots H_{i-1}$ if $i>1$ and, otherwise, $S_i=\mathbb{R}^d$
                \State Compute the solution $H_i$ of Pessimistic-ERM{} specified by tolerance $\rho=0$, positive
                \item[] \phantom{....}~~~~~~~ samples $P$, unlabeled samples $U\cap S_i$, and hypothesis class $\hypo{H}$
            \EndFor{}
            \vspace{2mm}
            \State \textbf{return} $H\coloneqq H_1\cap H_2\cap\dots\cap H_T.$
        \EndProcedure
        \end{algorithmic} \end{algorithm} 
        \noindent We divide the proof of correctness into two parts.
        
        \paragraph{Step A (Bounding the number of false negatives):}
            Each of $H_1,H_2,\dots,H_T$ is feasible for the Pessimistic-ERM{} constraint with tolerance $\rho=0$ and positive samples $P$ with $\abs{P}=n$.
            We claim that this implies that that with probability $1-\delta$, for each $1\leq i\leq k$, $\customcal{D}^\star\inparen{{H^\star}\setminus H_i}\leq O\inparen{\varepsilon^{2q}}\leq O(\varepsilon^2)$ (as $q\geq 1$).
            We proved this claim below and for now proceed with the proof.
            Since $H\coloneqq H_1\cap H_2\cap\dots\cap H_T$, an immediate consequence of the above is that with probability $1-\delta$, 
            \[
                \customcal{D}^\star\inparen{{H^\star}\setminus H}
                \leq \sum_i \customcal{D}^\star\inparen{{H^\star}\setminus H_i}
                \leq O\inparen{\frac{\varepsilon^2}{\varepsilon}}
                = O(\varepsilon)\,.
            \]

            \noindent \textit{Proof of Claim.}~~
            Next, we prove our earlier claim.
            Let $S\in\hypo{H}$ be any solution of Pessimistic-ERM{} with $\rho=0$.
            By feasibility, it satisfies $\nfrac{\abs{S \cap P}}{\abs{P}}=1$ and, hence, $\nfrac{\abs{ P\setminus S}}{\abs{P}}=0$.
            Due to the choice of the sample size $n$ and \cref{thm:unifConvergence}, with probability $1-\inparen{\nfrac{\delta}{2}}$, for each $R\in \hypo{H}\cup \inbrace{G^c\colon G\in \hypo{H}}$,\footnote{Here, we use the facts that $\textrm{\rm VC}{(\inbrace{G^c\colon G\in \hypo{H}})}=\textrm{\rm VC}{(\hypo{H})}$ and $\textrm{\rm VC}{(\hypo{H}_1\cup\hypo{H}_2)}\leq {\textrm{\rm VC}{(\hypo{H}_1)}+\textrm{\rm VC}{(\hypo{H}_2)}+1}$ \cite{mohri2018foundations}.}
            \[
                \customcal{P}^\star(R) 
                \leq 
                \frac{\abs{R\cap P}}{\abs{P}}
                +
                \sqrt{\frac{\abs{R\cap P}}{\abs{P}}\cdot \varepsilon}
                + \varepsilon\,.
            \]
            In particular, applying this to $R=S^c$ (note that $S^c\in\{G^c: G\in \hypo{H}\}$), and using $\nfrac{\abs{ P\cap S^c}}{\abs{P}}=\nfrac{\abs{ P\setminus S}}{\abs{P}}=0$, implies that 
            \[
                \customcal{P}^\star(S^c) \leq \varepsilon\,.
            \]
            Finally, since $\customcal{D}^\star( R )\leq \customcal{P}^\star( R )$ for any $ R \subseteq {H^\star}$, it follows that 
            \[
                \customcal{D}^\star({H^\star}\setminus  S)
                \leq \customcal{P}^\star({H^\star}\setminus  S )
                = \customcal{P}^\star(S^c)
                \leq  \varepsilon\,.
            \]  
        
        \paragraph{Step B (Bounding the number of false positives):}
            Next, we bound the amount of false positives.
            We claim that 
            \[
                \abs{U\setminus H_1}
                \geq 
                \abs{(U\cap H_1)\setminus H_2}
                \geq 
                \abs{(U\cap H_1\cap H_2)\setminus H_3}
                \geq 
                \dots 
                \geq 
                \abs{
                    (U\cap H_1\cap \dots \cap H_{T-1})
                    \setminus H_{T}
                }\,.
                \addtocounter{equation}{1}\tag{\theequation} \]
            To prove this, consider any $1\leq i\leq k-1$ and toward a contradiction suppose that 
            \[
                \abs{(U\cap H_1\cap \dots \cap H_{i-1})\setminus H_i}
                <
                \abs{(U\cap H_1\cap \dots \cap H_{i})\setminus H_{i+1}}\,.
                \addtocounter{equation}{1}\tag{\theequation} \]
            Hence, in particular,
            \begin{align*}
                \abs{(U\cap H_1\cap \dots \cap H_{i-1})\setminus H_{i+1}}
                ~\geq~ \abs{(U\cap H_1\cap \dots \cap H_{i})\setminus H_{i+1}}
                ~\Stackrel{\textup{\tagform@{\ref{eq:onesided:algo:contradiction}}}}{>}~ \abs{(U\cap H_1\cap \dots \cap H_{i-1})\setminus H_i}\,.
            \end{align*}
            This contradicts the fact $H_i$ is the optimal solution of Pessimistic-ERM{} defined by tolerance $\rho=0$, positive samples $P$, and unlabeled samples $U\cap H_1\cap \dots \cap H_{i-1}$.
            Therefore, due to the contradiction, our supposition in \cref{eq:onesided:algo:contradiction} must be wrong and, hence, \cref{eq:oneSided:monotone} is true.

            Next, we will use the above claim to conclude that $\abs{
                    (U\cap H_1\cap H_2\cap \dots \cap H_{T-1})
                    \setminus H_{T}
                }
                \leq \varepsilon\abs{U}$.
            Toward this, observe that the following collection of sets
            \[
                \inbrace{(U\cap H_1\cap H_2\cap \dots \cap H_{j})
                    \setminus H_{j+1} \mid 1\leq j\leq T}\,,
            \]
            is disjoint and, hence, $\sum_i \abs{(U\cap H_1\cap H_2\cap \dots \cap H_{i})}\leq \abs{U}$.
            This, along with \cref{eq:oneSided:monotone} implies that 
            \[
                \abs{
                    (U\cap H_1\cap H_2\cap \dots \cap H_{T-1})
                    \setminus H_{T}
                }
                ~~\leq~~ \frac{\abs{U}}{T}
                ~~~\Stackrel{(T=\nfrac{1}{\varepsilon})}{=}~~~ \varepsilon\abs{U}\,.
                \addtocounter{equation}{1}\tag{\theequation} \]
            \noindent Now, we are ready to prove the claim.
                    Consider the $T$-th instance of Pessimistic-ERM{} constructed in the above algorithm, \textit{i.e.}{}, the one defined by unlabeled samples $U\cap H_1\cap H_2\cap \dots \cap H_{T-1}$.
                    Since ${H^\star}\supseteq P$, ${H^\star}$ is feasible for this instance.
                    But since $H_{T}$ is the optimal solution of instance {$T$},
                    \[
                        \abs{U\cap H_1\cap H_2\cap \dots \cap H_{T-1} \cap {H^\star}}
                        \geq 
                        \abs{U\cap H_1\cap H_2\cap \dots \cap H_{T-1} \cap H_{T}}\,.
                    \]
                    Taking complements implies 
                    \[
                        \abs{U\cap H_1\cap H_2\cap \dots \cap H_{T-1} \setminus {H^\star}}
                        \leq 
                        \abs{U\cap H_1\cap H_2\cap \dots \cap H_{T-1} \setminus H_{T}}
                        ~~\Stackrel{\textup{\tagform@{\ref{eq:oneSided:upperBound}}}}{\leq}~~ 
                            \varepsilon \abs{U}\,.
                    \]
                    Since $H\subseteq H_1\cap H_2\cap \dots \cap H_{T}$, the above in particular implies that
                    \[
                        \abs{U\cap H \setminus {H^\star}}
                        \leq 
                        \abs{U\cap H_1\cap H_2\cap \dots \cap H_{T-1} \setminus {H^\star}}
                        \leq \varepsilon\abs{U}\,.
    \addtocounter{equation}{1}\tag{\theequation} \]
                    Now, second-order uniform convergence (\cref{thm:unifConvergence}) with respect to $U$ and the following hypothesis class 
                    \[
                        \hypo{H}_{\cap T} = \inbrace{G_1\cap G_2\cap \dots\cap G_{T}\setminus{H^\star}\colon G_1,G_2,\dots,G_{T} \in \hypo{H}}\,,
                    \]
                    implies that 
                    \[
                        \customcal{D}(H\setminus {H^\star}) \leq \varepsilon + \wt{O}\inparen{\sqrt{
                            \frac{\abs{U\cap H\setminus {H^\star}}}{\abs{U}}\cdot 
                            \frac{\textrm{\rm VC}{}\inparen{\hypo{H}_{\cap T}}+\log{\nfrac{1}{\delta}}}{n}}}
                        + \wt{O}\inparen{{\frac{\textrm{\rm VC}{}\inparen{\hypo{H}_{\cap T}}+\log{\nfrac{1}{\delta}}}{n}}}\,.
                    \]
                    Substituting the value of $n$, using that $\textrm{\rm VC}{}\inparen{\hypo{H}_{\cap T}}=\textrm{\rm VC}{{(\hypo{H})}}\cdot O(T\log{T})$, and $\nfrac{\abs{U\cap H\setminus{H^\star}}}{\abs{U}}\leq \varepsilon$ (from \cref{eq:oneSided:empiricalUB}) implies that 
                    \[
                        \customcal{D}(H\setminus {H^\star}) \leq \varepsilon + \wt{O}\inparen{\sqrt{
                            \varepsilon\cdot \frac{\textrm{\rm VC}{}(\hypo{H}) T +\log{\nfrac{1}{\delta}}}{n}}
                        }
                        + \wt{O}\inparen{
                            \frac{\textrm{\rm VC}{}(\hypo{H}) T+\log{\nfrac{1}{\delta}}}{n}
                        }
                        \leq O(\varepsilon)
                        \,.
                    \]
                    Therefore, \cref{asmp:smoothness}, implies 
                    \[
                        \customcal{D}^\star(H\setminus {H^\star})
                        \leq O(\nfrac{1}{\sigma})\cdot \varepsilon^{1/q}\,,
                    \]
                    completing the proof.

nodes.name: Proof outline of Theorem 3.3 assuming Theorem 4.3
nodes.statement:
The proof of \cref{thm:constReg} follows the strategy of the sample complexity proof (\cref{sec:perm}). 
        We iteratively construct instances of Pessimistic-ERM{} and define the final output as the intersection of the (approximate) solutions obtained at each iteration. 
        Compared to the sample complexity setting, several additional challenges arise since here we only find an approximate solution of the Pessimistic-ERM{} instances. 
        In particular, we must ensure that:
        \begin{enumerate}
            \item The hypothesis class $\hypo{H}$ remains well-approximated by low-degree polynomials with respect to the updated unlabeled distributions.
            \item The smoothness condition in \cref{asmp:smoothness} holds at every iteration.
        \end{enumerate}
        To address the former challenge, we include a check that the remaining region has at least a constant fraction of the mass. 
        To address the latter challenge, we also truncate the distribution of positive samples in addition to the distribution of unlabeled samples, and account for this in the analysis.
        Moreover, we truncate the distribution of positive samples and incorporate this modification into our analysis, ensuring that the surviving (\textit{i.e.}{}, non-truncated) region has sufficient mass to bound the runtime of obtaining samples from the truncated distributions via rejection sampling.

The proof of \cref{thm:constReg} follows the strategy of the sample complexity proof (\cref{sec:perm}). 
        We iteratively construct instances of Pessimistic-ERM{} and define the final output as the intersection of the (approximate) solutions obtained at each iteration.

nodes.name: Truncate positives to keep smoothness
nodes.statement:
To address the latter challenge, we also truncate the distribution of positive samples in addition to the distribution of unlabeled samples, and account for this in the analysis.
        Moreover, we truncate the distribution of positive samples and incorporate this modification into our analysis, ensuring that the surviving (\textit{i.e.}{}, non-truncated) region has sufficient mass to bound the runtime of obtaining samples from the truncated distributions via rejection sampling.

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 3.3
nodes.statement:
\paragraph{Proof of \cref{thm:main}.}
        We use the algorithm in \cref{alg:main}.
        First, we rescale $\varepsilon$ and $\delta$ to ensure that $\varepsilon\leq \nfrac{\alpha}{6}$ and $\delta\leq \sigma^2\varepsilon^{2q}$. 
        Due to the scaling in $\varepsilon$, the relation between $\zeta$ and $\varepsilon$ becomes $\zeta\leq O\binparen{(\sigma\varepsilon)^{5q^2}\alpha^{8q}}$ where $\varepsilon$ is the rescaled accuracy parameter, and we will use this updated relation in our analysis.
        Due to the scaling in $\delta$, the running time increases by logarithmic factors in $\max\inbrace{\nfrac{1}{\sigma},\nfrac{1}{\varepsilon^q}}$.
        The following constant shows up in our analysis:
        \[
            \gamma \coloneqq \sigma \varepsilon^q\,.
        \]
        \begin{algorithm}[htb!]
        \caption{\textsf{Iterative-}$\mathsf{Constrained\text{-}Regression}${} (from \cref{thm:main})}
        \begin{algorithmic}[1]
        \Procedure{\rm \textsf{Iterative-}$\mathsf{Constrained\text{-}Regression}${}}{$\varepsilon,\delta,\sigma,q,\alpha,k$}
            \vspace{2mm}
            \State {If $\varepsilon \geq \alpha$, set $\varepsilon=\nfrac{\alpha}{6}$}
            \State Set the accuracy parameters {$\zeta=O((\sigma\varepsilon)^{5q^2}\alpha^{8q})$} and $\gamma=\sigma^{-1}\varepsilon^{-q}$
            \State Set the number of iterations as $T=\nfrac{1}{\gamma}$
            \vspace{2mm}
            \vspace{2mm}
            \For{$1\leq i\leq T$}
                \State Define the survival set $S_i=H_1\cap H_2\cap\dots H_{i-1}$ if $i>1$ and, otherwise, $S_i=\mathbb{R}^d$
                \vspace{3mm}
                \item[] \phantom{.}\qquad~~ \textit{\#~~Step 1 (Ensure Low-Degree Approximation Exists)}
                \State Obtain $m=\wt{O}((\nfrac{1}{\gamma^3}) \cdot (d^k+\log{\nfrac{1}{\delta}}))$ samples $U$ from $\customcal{D}$ and $P$ from $\customcal{P}^\star$
                \If{$i > 1$ and either $\abs{U\cap S_i}\leq \gamma \abs{U}$ or $\abs{P\cap S_i}\leq (\nfrac{\alpha}{2})\abs{P}$} \State Break out of the for-loop
                \EndIf{}
                \vspace{3mm}
                \item[] \phantom{.}\qquad~~ \textit{\#~~Step 2 (Update Sample Distributions)}
                \State Define $\customcal{D}_i,\customcal{P}^\star_i,\customcal{D}^\star_i$ as the truncations of $\customcal{D},\customcal{P}^\star,\customcal{D}^\star$ to $S$
                \State Construct sampling oracles for $\customcal{D}_i$ and $\customcal{P}^\star_i$ via rejection sampling from $\customcal{D}$ and $\customcal{P}^\star$
                \vspace{3mm}
                \item[] \phantom{.}\qquad~~ \textit{\#~~Step 3 (Solve $i$-th Pessimistic-ERM{} Instance)}
                \State $H_i~\longleftarrow$~\hyperref[alg:constReg]{{\rm \textsf{Boosted-}}$\mathsf{Constrained\text{-}Regression}${}}($\zeta,\delta,\sigma,q,k$) with
                sample access to $\customcal{D}_i$ and $\customcal{P}^\star_i$
                \item[] \phantom{.}\qquad~~ \textit{\#~~Here, \hyperref[alg:constReg]{{\rm \textsf{Boosted-}}$\mathsf{Constrained\text{-}Regression}${}} is the algorithm referenced in \cref{thm:constReg}}
            \EndFor{}
            \vspace{2mm}
            \State \textbf{return} $H\coloneqq H_1\cap H_2\cap\dots\cap H_\ell$ where $\ell$ is the last iteration of the for-loop completed
        \EndProcedure
        \end{algorithmic} \end{algorithm} 
        
        \paragraph{Assumptions Required by \cref{thm:constReg} Hold.}
            We begin by proving that the assumptions required by \cref{thm:constReg} hold in each iteration where the for-loop executes.
            \begin{lemma} In each iteration $i$ where the for-loop in \cref{alg:main} executes, the following hold:
                \begin{enumerate}
                    \item Degree-$k$ polynomials $(\nfrac{\zeta}{\gamma})$-approximate $\hypo{H}$ with respect to  $\customcal{D}_i$ in $L_1$-norm. 
                    \item $(\customcal{D}^\star_i,\customcal{P}^\star_i,\customcal{D})$ is a valid PIU learning instance with constants $\sigma'\geq \nfrac{\alpha^2 \sigma}{3}$ and $q'=q$.
                \end{enumerate}
            \end{lemma}
            \begin{proof}[Proof of \cref{lem:main:assumptions}]
                Due to the guarantee of \cref{thm:constReg}, each of $H_1,H_2,\dots,H_T$ is a degree-$k$ PTF over $d$ variables.
                Since $S_i$ is an intersection of at most $T=\nfrac{1}{\gamma}$ sets from $H_1,H_2,\dots,H_T$, $S_i$ belongs to the family of the intersections of (at most) $\nfrac{1}{\gamma}$ degree-$k$ PTFs over $d$-variables, which has a VC dimension at most $\wt{O}(d^k/\gamma)$.
                Now, since the for-loop executes in the $i$-th iteration, the check in Step~\ref{step:alg:main:massCheck} ensures that with probability $1-\delta$, 
                \[
                    \customcal{D}(S_i)\geq \Omega({\gamma})
                    \quadtext{and}
                    \customcal{P}^\star(S_i)\geq \frac{\alpha}{2}-\gamma \geq \frac{\alpha}{3}\,,
                    \addtocounter{equation}{1}\tag{\theequation} \]
                due to uniform convergence over the class of (at most) $\nfrac{1}{\gamma}$ degree-$k$ PTFs over $d$-variables and $\gamma\leq \varepsilon \leq \nfrac{\alpha}{6}$.
                Further, since degree-$k$ polynomials $\zeta$-approximate $\hypo{H}$ with respect to  $\customcal{D}$ in $L_1$-norm, for every $H'\in \hypo{H}$, there is a degree-$k$ polynomial $p'\colon \mathbb{R}^d\to \mathbb{R}$ such that 
                \[
                    \operatornamewithlimits{\mathbb{E}}_{\customcal{D}}\insquare{\abs{p'(x) - \mathds{1}\sinbrace{x\in H'}}}\leq \zeta\,.
                \]
                Since $\customcal{D}(S_i)\geq \Omega(\gamma)$ and $\customcal{D}_i$ is the truncation of $\customcal{D}$ to $S_i$, a change of measure, implies 
                \[
                    \operatornamewithlimits{\mathbb{E}}_{\customcal{D}_i}\insquare{\abs{p'(x) - \mathds{1}\sinbrace{x\in H'}}}\leq O\inparen{\frac{\zeta}{\gamma}}\,.
                \]
                Since this holds for each $H'\in \hypo{H}$, the first result follows.

                To prove the second claim, it suffices to show that $\customcal{P}^\star_i$ is the truncation of $\customcal{D}^\star_i$ to the set ${H^\star}$ (which holds by construction) and that $\customcal{D}_i$ and $\customcal{D}^\star_i$ satisfy \cref{asmp:smoothness} with the specified constants.
                To prove the latter, consider any measurable set $T\subseteq \mathbb{R}^d$.
                Observe that due to \cref{asmp:smoothness}
                \[
                    \customcal{D}^\star_i(T)
                    = \frac{\customcal{D}^\star(T\cap S_i)}{\customcal{D}^\star(S_i)}
                    \leq \frac{\customcal{D}(T\cap S_i)^{1/q}}{\sigma\cdot \customcal{D}^\star(S_i)}
                    \leq \frac{3\cdot \customcal{D}(T\cap S_i)^{1/q}}{\sigma \alpha^2}
                    \,.
                \]
                Where in the last inequality we used \cref{eq:main:massGuarantee} and the fact that $\customcal{D}^\star(S_i)\geq \customcal{D}^\star({H^\star})\customcal{P}^\star(S_i)\geq \alpha\customcal{P}^\star(S_i)$ (due to \cref{asmp:posFraction}).
                We can continue the above chain of inequalities as follows 
                \[
                    \customcal{D}^\star_i(T)
                    \leq \frac{3}{\sigma\alpha^2} \cdot 
                        \inparen{\frac{\customcal{D}(T\cap S_i)}{\customcal{D}(S_i)}}^{1/q}
                    = \frac{3}{\sigma\alpha^2}\cdot \customcal{D}_i(T)^{1/q}\,.
                \]
            \end{proof}
        
        \paragraph{Guarantee of \cref{thm:constReg}.}
        
        To show correctness, we have to show that with probability $1-\delta$, $\customcal{D}^\star({H^\star}\triangle H)\leq \varepsilon$. 
        Since the required assumptions hold (\cref{lem:main:assumptions}), for each iteration $1\leq i\leq T$ executed, \cref{thm:constReg} implies the following guarantees:
        \begin{align*}
            \customcal{D}^\star_i({H^\star}\setminus H_i) 
                \leq O\inparen{\frac{1}{\sigma\alpha^2}}\cdot \inparen{\frac{\zeta}{\gamma}}^{1/(4q)}
                \quadtext{and}
            \customcal{D}_i(H_i) 
                &\leq \ensuremath{\mathrm{OPT}}_{\rm PERM}(i) + O\inparen{\frac{1}{\sigma\alpha^2}}\cdot \inparen{\frac{\zeta}{\gamma}}^{1/(4q)} + O(\delta)\,.
        \end{align*}
        Where $\ensuremath{\mathrm{OPT}}_{\rm PERM}(i)\coloneqq \min_{H\in \hypo{H}\,\colon\,\customcal{P}^\star_i(H)=1}\customcal{D}_i(H)$ is the optimal value of the $i$-th instance of Pessimistic-ERM{} in \cref{alg:main}.
        Since we ensured that $\zeta\leq O((\sigma\varepsilon)^{5q^2}\alpha^{8q})\leq  \gamma^{1+4q}\cdot (\sigma\alpha^2)^{4q}$ and $\delta\leq \gamma^2$, the above simplify to 
        \begin{align*}
            \customcal{D}^\star_i({H^\star}\setminus H_i) 
                \leq \gamma^2
                \quadtext{and}
            \customcal{D}_i(H_i) 
                &\leq \ensuremath{\mathrm{OPT}}_{\rm PERM}(i) + \gamma^2\,.
                \addtocounter{equation}{1}\tag{\theequation} \end{align*} 
        in the remainder of the proof, we condition on the event that the above inequalities hold. 

        \paragraph{Correctness.}
        Now, we are ready to complete the proof of correctness of \cref{alg:main}.
            We consider two cases depending on whether the for-loop exits.

            \itparagraph{Case A (For-loop breaks at iteration $i$):}
            First, suppose that the if statement first broke at step $i$, then the check in Step~\ref{step:alg:main:massCheck} (along with uniform convergence; as discussed in \cref{lem:main:assumptions}) implies that $\customcal{D}(S_i)=\customcal{D}(H_1\cap H_2\cap\dots H_{i-1})\leq O(\gamma)$ and $H=H_1\cap H_2\cap\dots H_{i-1}$.
            Therefore, $\customcal{D}(H\setminus {H^\star})\leq \customcal{D}(H)\leq O(\gamma)$. 
            Applying \cref{asmp:smoothness} yields $\customcal{D}^\star(H \setminus {H^\star}) \leq \sigma^{-1}\cdot \gamma^{1/q}\leq \varepsilon$.
            Further, since all previous iterations $1,2,\dots,i-1$, the for-loop executed, \cref{eq:main:constRegGuarantee} holds and implies that 
            $\customcal{D}^\star({H^\star}\setminus H)\leq \sum_{j=1}^{i-1} \customcal{D}^\star({H^\star}\setminus H_i)\leq (i-1)\gamma^2\leq \gamma\leq \varepsilon$ where we used that $i\leq T=\nfrac{1}{\gamma}$.
            Combining these bounds implies that 
            \[
                \customcal{D}^\star({H^\star}\triangle H)\leq 2\varepsilon\,,
            \]
            completing the proof of correctness in this case.

            \itparagraph{Case B (For-loop never breaks):}
            Now, we consider the other case, where the break condition is never satisfied and, hence, all $T$ iterations of the for loop take place.
            \begin{align*}
                \customcal{D}^\star({H^\star}\setminus H)~~
                &\leq~~ \sum_i \customcal{D}^\star\sinparen{{H^\star}\cap H_1 \cap H_2 \cap \dots \cap H_{i-1}\setminus H_i}\\
                &\leq~~ \sum_i \customcal{D}^\star\sinparen{{H^\star}\setminus H_i}\\
                &\Stackrel{\textup{\tagform@{\ref{eq:main:constRegGuarantee}}}}{\leq}~~ 
                    \gamma\,. 
                    \tagnum{since $T=\nfrac{1}{\gamma}$}{eq:computational:caseB}
            \end{align*}
            To finish the proof of correctness in Case B, we need to bound $\customcal{D}^\star(H \setminus {H^\star})$. 
            For this, we will use the following claim to bound $\customcal{D}(H \setminus {H^\star})$, and then apply \cref{asmp:smoothness}.
            \begin{claim} It holds that 
                \begin{align*}
                    \customcal{D}(\mathbb{R}^d\setminus H_1)
                    &\geq \customcal{D}(H_1\setminus H_2) - \gamma^2\\
                    &\geq \customcal{D}(H_1\cap H_2\setminus H_3) - 2\gamma^2\\
                    &~~\vdots\\
                    &\geq \customcal{D}(H_1\cap H_2\cap \dots H_{T-1}\setminus H_T) - (T-1)\gamma^2\,.
                \end{align*}
            \end{claim}
            \begin{proof}[Proof of \cref{lem:main:chaining}]
                Toward a contradiction, suppose that for some index $i$
                \[
                    \customcal{D}(H_1\cap H_2\cap \dots \cap H_i\setminus H_{i+1})
                    > \customcal{D}(H_1\cap H_2\cap \dots \cap H_{i-1}\setminus H_{i}) + \gamma^2\,.
                \]
                Replacing the intersection on the LHS from $H_1\cap H_2\cap \dots \cap H_i$ to $H_1\cap H_2\cap \dots \cap H_{i-1}$, implies
                \[
                    \customcal{D}(H_1\cap H_2\cap \dots \cap H_{i-1}\setminus H_{i+1})
                    > \customcal{D}(H_1\cap H_2\cap \dots \cap H_{i-1}\setminus H_{i}) + \gamma^2\,.
                \]
                Equivalently, 
                \[
                    \customcal{D}_{H_1\cap H_2\cap \dots \cap H_{i-1}}(\mathbb{R}^d\setminus H_{i+1})
                    > \customcal{D}_{H_1\cap H_2\cap \dots \cap H_{i-1}}(\mathbb{R}^d\setminus H_{i}) 
                        + \frac{\gamma^2}{\customcal{D}(H_1\cap H_2\cap \dots \cap H_{i-1})}\,.
                \]
                Since $\customcal{D}(H_1\cap H_2\cap \dots \cap H_{i-1})\geq \Omega(\gamma)$ due to \cref{lem:main:assumptions}, the above implies that 
                \[
                    \customcal{D}_{H_1\cap H_2\cap \dots \cap H_{i-1}}(\mathbb{R}^d\setminus H_{i+1})
                    > \customcal{D}_{H_1\cap H_2\cap \dots \cap H_{i-1}}(\mathbb{R}^d\setminus H_{i}) 
                        + O(\gamma)\,.
                \]
                Taking complements, we get 
                \[
                    \customcal{D}_{H_1\cap H_2\cap \dots \cap H_{i-1}}(H_{i}) 
                    > \customcal{D}_{H_1\cap H_2\cap \dots \cap H_{i-1}}(H_{i+1})
                        + O(\gamma)\,.
                \]
                This contradicts \cref{eq:main:constRegGuarantee} (at the $i$-th step) since $H_{i+1}$ is feasible for the $i$-th instance of Pessimistic-ERM{} constructed by \cref{alg:main} and, hence, $\customcal{D}_{H_1\cap H_2\cap \dots \cap H_{i-1}}(H_{i+1})\geq \ensuremath{\mathrm{OPT}}_{\rm PERM}(i)$.
            \end{proof}
            Now we will use \cref{lem:main:chaining} to bound $\customcal{D}(H\setminus{H^\star})$. 
            Since the sets $\inbrace{H_1\cap H_2\cap\dots \cap H_{i-1}\setminus H_i}_i$ are disjoint, it follows that 
            \[
                T\cdot \customcal{D}(H_1\cap H_2\cap \dots \cap H_{T-1} \setminus H_T)
                - T(T-1)\gamma^2
                \leq \sum_i \customcal{D}(H_1 \cap H_2 \cap \dots \cap H_{i-1}\setminus H_i)
                \leq 1\,.
            \]
            Therefore, 
            \begin{align*}
                \customcal{D}(H_1\cap H_2\cap \dots \cap H_{T-1}\setminus H_T)
                \leq \frac{1}{T} + (T-1)\gamma^2
                \leq 2\gamma\,.
                \addtocounter{equation}{1}\tag{\theequation} \end{align*}
            Apart from this, as $\customcal{D}_{H_1\cap H_2\cap \dots \cap H_{T-1}}(H_T)\leq \ensuremath{\mathrm{OPT}}_{\rm PERM}(T)+\gamma^2$ and ${H^\star}$ is feasible for the $T$-th instance of Pessimistic-ERM{} (so $\customcal{D}_{H_1\cap H_2\cap \dots \cap H_{T-1}}({H^\star})\geq \ensuremath{\mathrm{OPT}}_{\rm PERM}(T)$), the following also holds
            \[
                \customcal{D}_{H_1\cap H_2\cap \dots \cap H_{T-1}}(H_T)
                \leq 
                \customcal{D}_{H_1\cap H_2\cap \dots \cap H_{T-1}}({H^\star})
                + \gamma^2\,.
            \]
            and consequently, 
            \[
                \customcal{D}(H_1\cap H_2\cap \dots \cap H_{T-1}\setminus {H^\star})
                \leq 
                \customcal{D}(H_1\cap H_2\cap \dots \cap H_{T-1}\setminus H_T)
                + \gamma^2\,.
                \addtocounter{equation}{1}\tag{\theequation} \]
            Hence,
            \[
                \customcal{D}(H \setminus {H^\star})
                \leq 
                \customcal{D}(H_1\cap H_2\cap \dots \cap H_{T-1}\setminus {H^\star})
                ~~~\Stackrel{\textup{\tagform@{\ref{eq:main:chainingGuarantee}}},~\textup{\tagform@{\ref{eq:main:optimalityGuaranteeTth}}}}{\leq}~~~  
                \gamma^2 + 2\gamma
                \leq 3\gamma\,.
            \]
        Applying \cref{asmp:smoothness}, we have $\customcal{D}^\star(H \setminus {H^\star}) \leq \sigma^{-1} \cdot \customcal{D}(H \setminus {H^\star})^{1/q} \leq \sigma^{-1} \cdot (3\gamma)^{1/q}\leq 3\varepsilon$. 
        Combining this with \textup{\tagform@{\ref{eq:computational:caseB}}} implies that 
        \[
            \customcal{D}^\star({H^\star}\triangle H)\leq 2\varepsilon\,,
        \]
        completing the proof of correctness in Case B.
        
    

    \paragraph{Computational Efficiency.}
        Finally, it remains to show that \cref{alg:main} runs in sample polynomial time.
        
        \begin{lemma} Consider the setting of \cref{thm:main}. \cref{alg:main} runs in time $\mathrm{poly}(n)$ with probability $1-\delta$ where $n=\mathrm{poly}(d^k,\nfrac{1}{\zeta},\log{\nfrac{1}{\delta}})$.
        \end{lemma}
        \begin{proof}[Proof of \cref{lem:main:rejectionSampling}]
            The only computationally non-trivial step in \cref{alg:main} is the call to boosted constraint regression and the construction of and sampling from distributions $\customcal{D}_i$ and $\customcal{P}^\star_i$ via rejection sampling.
            Since the assumptions of \cref{thm:sampleComplexity} hold (see \cref{lem:main:assumptions}), it promises that the call to boosted constraint regression is efficient and runs in time $\mathrm{poly}(d^k,\nfrac{1}{\zeta},\log{\nfrac{1}{\delta}})$. 
            Hence, it remains to bound the time of rejection sampling.
            
            For this, it suffices to show a lower bound on the mass of $\customcal{D}(S_i)$ and $\customcal{P}^\star(S_i)$ for each $i$ so that it is not too small, since the inverse of this quantity is the expected number of samples from $\customcal{D}$ and $\customcal{P}^\star$ one would need to see a single sample in $S_i$. 
            We already proved this in \cref{eq:main:massGuarantee}. 
            In particular, the bounds in \cref{eq:main:massGuarantee} ensure that each call to the sampling oracle in \cref{alg:main}, with probability $1-\eta$, runs in time $O((\nfrac{1}{\varepsilon})\log{\nfrac{1}{\eta}})$ (for any $\eta\in(0,1)$). 
            Selecting $\eta$ to be a suitably small multiple of $\delta$ and taking a union bound over $\mathrm{poly}(d^k,\nfrac{1}{\zeta},\log{\nfrac{1}{\delta}})$ calls implies the claim with only a logarithmic increase in the running time.

        \end{proof}

nodes.name: Proof of Claim 4.5
nodes.statement:
Toward a contradiction, suppose that for some index $i$
                \[
                    \customcal{D}(H_1\cap H_2\cap \dots \cap H_i\setminus H_{i+1})
                    > \customcal{D}(H_1\cap H_2\cap \dots \cap H_{i-1}\setminus H_{i}) + \gamma^2\,.

                Replacing the intersection on the LHS from $H_1\cap H_2\cap \dots \cap H_i$ to $H_1\cap H_2\cap \dots \cap H_{i-1}$, implies
                \[
                    \customcal{D}(H_1\cap H_2\cap \dots \cap H_{i-1}\setminus H_{i+1})
                    > \customcal{D}(H_1\cap H_2\cap \dots \cap H_{i-1}\setminus H_{i}) + \gamma^2\,.
                \]
                Equivalently, 
                \[
                    \customcal{D}_{H_1\cap H_2\cap \dots \cap H_{i-1}}(\mathbb{R}^d\setminus H_{i+1})
                    > \customcal{D}_{H_1\cap H_2\cap \dots \cap H_{i-1}}(\mathbb{R}^d\setminus H_{i}) 
                        + \frac{\gamma^2}{\customcal{D}(H_1\cap H_2\cap \dots \cap H_{i-1})}\,.

                Since $\customcal{D}(H_1\cap H_2\cap \dots \cap H_{i-1})\geq \Omega(\gamma)$ due to \cref{lem:main:assumptions}, the above implies that 
                \[

                    > \customcal{D}_{H_1\cap H_2\cap \dots \cap H_{i-1}}(\mathbb{R}^d\setminus H_{i}) 
                        + O(\gamma)\,.
